# Biological Specimens
[color=#a4885c]RESTRICTED. Research staff only. The contents of this section may not be shared with anyone who isn't cleared for it, including other Company employees.[/color]
The frontier holds organisms the Company considers of great scientific and medical value. Some are dangerous. Research staff may be asked to study them. This section exists so staff can recognise them and stay safe.
## Organisms of Interest - [bold]XX-121 ("Xenomorph")[/bold]: a hostile, hive-building organism. Its blood is a strong acid that damages most materials. It reproduces through a parasitic larval stage. Any egg, larva or parasite is to be treated as a live and dangerous specimen. - [bold]Biomorph tissue[/bold]: an aggressive mass of living flesh that spreads through venom and spores. All tissue and venom samples are an infection risk. - [bold]Variant organisms[/bold]: the Company has recorded several related or unusual forms, including the [bold]Neomorph[/bold] and the large predator known as the [bold]Wendigo[/bold]. Any unfamiliar organism is to be treated as dangerous until the Lead Researcher says otherwise.
## Live Specimens - Research staff may not approach a live specimen. Live specimens are collected and moved by specialist Company teams. - Specimens are delivered sedated and restrained in a secure specimen crate. - A specimen crate may only be opened on the Lead Researcher's instruction, and never with only one person present. - A sedated specimen is to be kept sedated. If it starts to move, staff must leave, seal the area and call Security.
## Samples and Remains - Dead specimens and tissue remain hazardous. Acid blood stays active after death, and biomorph tissue can still infect. - Every sample must be logged, labelled and stored under lock. - Specimen data may not be stored anywhere outside the laboratory. - Samples may only be destroyed on the Lead Researcher's instruction, and the destruction must be recorded.
## Public Knowledge - Colonists aren't aware these organisms exist. Staff may not tell them. - A colonist who asks about something they have seen is to be told the matter is under investigation, and referred to the Corporate Liaison. - The Company's work with these organisms is carried out for the benefit of science and medicine. Questions about the wider programme are to be put to the Lead Researcher, who will answer as far as the staff member's clearance allows.
